q: A new project is starting. When should the team look at lessons learned from similar past projects?
options: At closure, to compare results with them
At the start, to plan and identify risks
Only if a serious problem happens later on in the project
Never, since each project is unique
explanation: Lessons learned from previous projects can be used in the current project; the lessons learned register is an input to planning processes such as Identify Risks and Estimate Costs.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Lessons learned register

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Lessons learned register

q: Which document records the situation, impacts, recommendations and proposed actions of each lesson during the project?
options: The issue log for the project
The change log
The risk report
The lessons learned register
explanation: The lessons learned register may include the category and description of the situation, its impacts, recommendations and proposed actions.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Lessons learned register

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Lessons learned register

q: When is the lessons learned register first created?
options: Early, in Manage Project Knowledge
Only at the end, in Close Project or Phase
When the first audit takes place
After the final report has been accepted by the sponsor
explanation: The register is created as an output of Manage Project Knowledge early in the project, then used and updated in many processes throughout.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Lessons learned register

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Lessons learned register

q: During an 18-month project, the team writes down no lessons until the final week. What has been lost?
options: Nothing, since final lessons are always complete
The lessons can no longer be archived
Lessons could have improved this project too
The sponsor will refuse the final report later
explanation: Managing knowledge is more than obtaining lessons at the end. Captured throughout, lessons improve the current project as well as future ones.

q: Which four questions structure an after-action review?
options: Who, what, where and when did it happen?
What was planned, what happened, why, what can we learn?
What did it cost, who paid, who approved, who signed?
Which risks, which owners, which triggers, which reserves?
explanation: AARs ask: what was supposed to happen, what actually happened, why were there differences, and what can we learn?

q: A project wants to review its performance at several stages instead of only at the end. Which technique fits?
options: A post-implementation audit only
A final postmortem
A bidder conference
In-progress postmortems
explanation: In-progress postmortems are structured reviews at various stages of the life cycle, unlike traditional postmortems at the end, so problems are solved in time.

q: A senior engineer's know-how is hard to write down. Which techniques help pass it on?
options: Storytelling and work shadowing
A longer lessons learned template
A change request to the PMO
A larger risk register with more fields
explanation: Tacit knowledge is hard to codify; storytelling is effective for transferring it, and knowledge management tools such as work shadowing connect people.

q: Why does the Agile Practice Guide call the retrospective possibly the most important agile practice?
options: It sets the team's velocity target
It replaces the sprint review
It lets the team learn about and improve its process
It lets managers rate each team member's performance
explanation: The retrospective allows the team to learn about, improve and adapt its process: at regular intervals it reflects on how to become more effective.

q: A retrospective produces fifteen improvement ideas. What does the Agile Practice Guide advise?
options: Start all fifteen at once in the next iteration
Limit actions to what the team can finish
Give all of them to the scrum master
Wait for the next release to choose any
explanation: Limit action items to the team's capacity; trying to improve too much at once and finishing nothing is much worse than completing fewer items.

q: How does a team know whether an improvement from its retrospective worked?
options: By asking the sponsor's opinion
By counting the action items
By repeating the same retrospective twice
By measuring the agreed outcome later
explanation: When the team selects improvements, it decides how to measure the outcomes, then measures them in the next period to validate success or failure.

q: In a retrospective, one member blames a colleague for a missed deadline. What should the facilitator do?
options: Refocus on learning, not blame
Record the blame in the minutes
End the retrospective at once
Ask the team to vote on who was at fault in the end
explanation: A retrospective is not about blame; it needs a psychologically safe space where everyone can speak candidly without fear of blame or retaliation.

q: Which of these is a continuous improvement approach named in the PMBOK Guide?
options: Critical path method
Earned value analysis
Plan-do-check-act
Rolling wave planning
explanation: Continuous improvement can use PDCA, Lean, Total Quality Management, Six Sigma, the Five Focusing Steps and similar methods.

q: The company's risk checklist still lists a technology the company no longer uses. What should happen?
options: Keep it, since checklists never change
Review the checklist and archive obsolete items
Stop using checklists altogether
Add a note about it to the project's issue log only
explanation: Checklists should be reviewed from time to time to add new information and remove or archive obsolete information.

q: A team finds a better way to run its code reviews. How can the improvement be made to last?
options: Hope that everyone remembers it later
Mention it once in the daily meeting
Keep it a secret from all of the other teams
Update the working agreements and plan
explanation: Process improvement changes the process itself; recording it in the plan and the team's working agreements keeps it in place, and sharing it adds to organizational learning.

q: Who usually owns and changes the organization's project templates and procedures?
options: The PMO or another function, through policy
Each project team, freely, as it wishes
The project's external vendor
The sponsor of whichever project is running now
explanation: Policies, processes and procedures are usually established by the PMO or another function outside the project and updated only by following organizational policies.

q: Which organizational process assets does the project team itself update throughout the project?
options: The company's whole procurement policy
The PMO's standard project templates
The organizational knowledge repositories
The national regulations
explanation: Knowledge repositories (financial performance, lessons learned, metrics, issues and defects) are updated throughout the project with project information.

q: Midway through, the team finds that the company's estimating template misses a common cost item. What should the project manager do?
options: Quietly edit the company template for everyone
Tell the template's owner and suggest the change
Ignore it, since templates belong to the PMO
Stop using estimates until it is fixed
explanation: Templates change through organizational policy, so improvement suggestions go to the owning unit; the project can record the gap as a lesson and handle it in its own estimates.

q: Which processes list organizational process asset updates among their outputs?
options: Develop Schedule, Estimate Costs and Develop Budget
Plan Scope Management and Define Scope
Identify Stakeholders and Acquire Resources
Manage Project Knowledge and Close Project or Phase
explanation: Figures 2-8 and 2-12 list OPA updates among the outputs of Manage Project Knowledge and Close Project or Phase.

q: What is a community of practice for?
options: Sharing knowledge among people with common interests
Approving or rejecting changes to the project's baselines
Auditing the project's financial records
Selecting vendors for procurement
explanation: Communities of practice (or interest) are knowledge management tools that connect people to share tacit knowledge and create new knowledge.

q: Besides the end of an iteration, when might a team hold a retrospective?
options: Only at the very end of the whole project
Only when the sponsor requests one
When the team is stuck and work is not flowing
Never outside the agreed iteration schedule at all
explanation: Teams may retrospect after a release, when weeks have passed, when the team appears stuck and work is not flowing, or at any milestone.

q: Which kind of knowledge do information management tools share best?
options: Tacit knowledge held in experts' minds
Simple, codified explicit knowledge
Personal intuition and experience
Unwritten team norms and habits
explanation: Information management tools are effective for sharing simple, unambiguous, codified explicit knowledge, such as lessons learned entries and library services.

q: Which of these belongs in a lessons learned entry, according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: The names of the people who made the mistakes
The team's salaries and bonuses
The vendor's private cost data
Impacts, recommendations and proposed actions
explanation: The register may include the category and description of the situation, impacts, recommendations and proposed actions.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Lessons learned register

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Lessons learned register

q: How does a continuous improvement mindset benefit the organization, according to the Standard?
options: It grows maturity across the whole organization
It removes the need for any project planning at all
It guarantees every project is on schedule
It replaces quality control on deliverables
explanation: A continuous improvement mindset optimizes processes, boosts efficiency and enhances maturity growth for the whole organization.

q: How do quality audits contribute to continuous improvement?
options: By assigning blame for defects to individuals
By approving the project's final budget
By sharing good practices from similar projects
By replacing the lessons learned register entirely
explanation: Quality audit objectives include sharing good practices from similar projects, helping improve processes, and adding contributions to the lessons learned repository.

q: How can GenAI tools support retrospectives, according to the Agile Practice Guide?
options: By deciding the team's improvements for it
By anonymizing notes and tracking actions
By rating each member's contribution
By replacing the facilitator entirely
explanation: GenAI tools can read notes and boards, anonymize text, suggest small experiments and track actions over time.

q: Which THREE are tools and techniques of Manage Project Knowledge?
options: After-action reviews
Storytelling
Retrospective meetings
Earned value analysis
Make-or-buy analysis
Critical path method
explanation: Figure 2-8 lists expert judgment, knowledge and information management, after-action reviews, in-progress postmortems, storytelling, retrospective meetings and interpersonal skills.

q: Which TWO are continuous improvement approaches named in the PMBOK Guide?
options: Six Sigma
Lean
Fast tracking
Crashing
Rolling wave planning
explanation: PDCA, Lean, Total Quality Management, Six Sigma and the Five Focusing Steps are named; the others are scheduling techniques.

q: Which TWO are knowledge management tools that connect people with each other?
options: Communities of practice
Work shadowing
Library services
Web searches
Codified register entries
explanation: Knowledge management connects people (networking, communities of practice, shadowing, forums). Library services, searches and codified entries are information management.

q: Match each technique with how it works.
right: The team reflects at least each iteration
Planned versus actual, why, and lessons
A structured review at various stages
Narratives that pass on tacit knowledge
explanation: All four feed the lessons learned register and continuous improvement; retrospectives are frequent, AARs follow milestones, postmortems run in progress, stories carry tacit knowledge.

q: Complete each statement about continuous improvement.

blanks.text: Knowledge gained during a project to improve future performance is called
OPAs that the project updates throughout are the

explanation: Lessons learned improve future work; the project updates knowledge repositories; PDCA is a continuous improvement cycle.
